messages.subject: Allometry
parts:
Dear all,

I have some doubts regarding the analysis of allometry. Im studying the wing shape differences of a cicada genus. My species have unique allometries, this is my code:




predline plot of the allometric analysis, slopes look quite different



the pairwise comparisons for slope vector length shows differences in 5 out of 66 pairwise comparisons, involving 3 species. 

 but the angle pairwise comparisons dont show any significant differences although most angles are >50º. 



My first question is why isnt there any significant differences in angle, when they look so different both in the plot and the pairwise comparison?
My second question, regards the best way to conduct my analysis. Since the differences between slopes are so few and involving only 3 species, is it appropriate to analyse the differences between the other species fitting a common slope model and analysed the 3 species allometric trajectories separately (my intuition says no!)? Alternatively, can i use trajectory analysis to explore how each species shape changes with size? Is there other way, to explore different allometric trajectories? Most literature i have found deals with ontogenic allometry and not evolutionary allometry, so any insight would be appreciated.

Thank you for your time.



Raquel Mendes

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Allometry
parts:
Raquel,

What was the effect size of the interaction for the unique allometries model?  Predline plots can be misleading without associated statistics. 

It is possible -especially with so many slopes - that many non-significantly different slopes compile to an overall significant effect. But then a small effect size should be apparent. 

Can you share the ANOVA tables?

Cheers!
Mike

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Allometry
parts:
Raquel,

I find it curious that you got different results (the interaction Z-score and P-value should have been the same as the ANOVA between the two models), but let’s table that one for a moment.  The amount of variation explained by unique allometries is 3%.  The species differences account for 15% of the shape variation.  Nobody is obligated to choose a model based on a significance criterion if the effect size is small.  In your shoes, I would choose the common allometry model and compare species LS means (mean shape at mean size), not worrying about this little effect.  I think you are justified to say the a common allometry model is the model you want to work with.

Also, I would trust the anova(fit.unique) results and not the anova(fit.common, fit.unique).  Something is wrong there, and it seems emergent.  I will have to debug that code.  So thank you for your example, as it found a problem!

Finally, the anova(fit.size, fit.species) result you found was much more impressive because the former model has one slope, the latter model has each species intercept and unique slope, meaning it confounds species means and slopes.  Of course there is a significant difference because species means are different (but you cannot tell it is that or slopes without further investigation).  You now know species means are different and allometric variation does not complicate this inference.

Hope that helps!
Mike
